software.description: The documented data-preparation workflow imports the Firm X and Firm Y files into SAS. The registered environment metadata reports SAS status unverified (return code 1, no version token); this does not establish that SAS is absent. No SAS process was started, and the author release/version is unspecified.

software.name: Stata
software.description: The registered environment probe reports Stata 18 available. The narrative describes Stata analyses using mixed and gsem, but no executable commands are supplied and the authors' release is unspecified, so command-level compatibility and exact model syntax remain unverified.

issues.description: The package contains a prose data description but no supplied executable program or complete analysis script. The authors explicitly state that they cannot provide the computer programs used. The documented SAS preparation and Stata analyses therefore cannot be launched from this release.

The documents name author data tables and describe panel construction, pooling, winsorization, sample selection, and analyses, but none of the inputs or outputs is supplied. Exact coverage, remaining mappings and definitions, table specifications, and an authorized route to the full author data remain unverified. The narrative is not executable code, so closure cannot be established from it.

The narrative references Section 3.3 for the sufficient-audit-work sample threshold but does not include that section. It identifies model families and datasets for tables but does not provide the complete equations, covariate lists, estimation commands, or output-generation instructions. Exact year coverage and some source value/category fields are also unspecified, so the prose alone cannot establish complete producer/consumer closure.

The narrative first describes firmXpanel.csv as an imported source panel and later uses firmXpanel.csv as the final Firm X dataset after joining firmXtotal.csv. The aggregate-input table lists firmXtotal.csv in the prose but labels its variable-name column as firmXpanel.csv. The absent program leaves the input/output paths and aggregate field association unresolved.

evidence.description: The authors describe proprietary data kept in a secure virtual environment with no export capability.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
Our study utilizes data provided to us by the Foundation for Auditing Research (FAR) in
accordance with the signed agreement we executed with the FAR for project number 2017B06
Ciconte. The data are proprietary and confidential and the authors could only access the data in a
virtual environment with no ability to export any data, output, or code from the environment. As
a result, we are complying with the "Data and Code Sharing Policy for the Journal of
Accounting Research” by providing detailed step-by-step descriptions of the relevant code
written to conduct the analyses.

evidence.description: The registered inventory lists only the two author documents; no data tables or programs are included.
The narrative names additional Firm X source fields used to construct derived measures.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
Using these data, we then construct several additional measures. We generate an indicator
variable, BIG_MKT, using variable “officeid”. We generate AUTO, CONSUMER, TELECOM,
FS, GOVERNMENT, SERVICES, CHEMICAL, ENERGY, CONSTRUCTION, HEALTHCARE,
TRANSPORTATION, MANUFACTURING, and OTHER using the variable “industry”. We
generate the variables DIRECTOR and PARTNER using the variable “rank”. In order to generate
the variable CONSULT_OTHER we subtract “consultacc” and “consultas” from
“numberconsult” and then log transform this difference.

evidence.description: The narrative names the Firm X aggregate input and its year join.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
Next, we import the file firmXtotal.csv into SAS. This file contains aggregate data at the firm
level for Firm X and includes the following variables:

 Label in Appendix A                               Variable Name in File firmXpanel.csv
 FIRMPFT                                           totalprofit
 FIRMAF                                            totalauditfees
 FIRMNAF                                           totalnonauditfees
 FIRMPUBLIC                                        totalpublic


We join these data with firmXpanel.csv using the unique year identifiers to arrive at our final
data set for Firm X. The variable for year in file firmXpanel.csv is “fiscalyear” while the variable

evidence.description: The narrative names risk.csv, its auditor/year keys and a risk-rating aggregation.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
1. We import the file risk.csv which contains risk ratings for each individual audit client of
      the individual auditors in our sample for each year. Each row has a unique “staffcode”
      and “fiscalyear”. We then compute the average risk rating in SAS by unique auditor
      (using the variable “staffcode”) and year (using the variable “fiscalyear”) to compute
      “clientrisk” which corresponds to RISK in Appendix A. We then join these ratings with
      panelY.csv using variables “staffcode” and “fiscalyear”.

evidence.description: The narrative names reviews.csv and describes review aggregation and the reviewratio construction.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
across both datasets. The file reviews.csv pertains to external reviews and contains a
      unique identifier for each auditor “staffcode” for each year as identified with the variable
      “fiscalyear”. We merge reviews.csv with the merged dataset for internal reviews and
      aggregate the number of total reviews “total” as well as compliant reviews “compliant”
      by auditor using the variable “staffcode” and year using the variable “fiscalyear”. We

evidence.description: The narrative names consult.csv and describes auditor/year consultation and opinion measures.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
3. We import the dataset consult.csv which contains data on modified opinions and
      consultations. There is a unique identifier for each auditor “staffcodeel” and a unique
      year as indicated with the variable “fy”. We aggregate these data by auditor and year to

   construct measures of the number of total consultations “consult”, technical accounting
   consultations “accounting” which corresponds to CONSULT_ACC in Appendix A,
   auditing standard consultations “auditing” which corresponds to CONSULT_AUD in
   Appendix A, other consultations “other” which corresponds to CONSULT_OTHER in
   Appendix A, and modified opinions “modop” which corresponds to MODOP in
   Appendix A. We set any variables with missing values equal to 0. We merge these data
   with the panel dataset panelY.csv where “staffcode” is equal to “staffcodeel” and
   “fiscalyear” is equal to “fy”.

evidence.quote:
4. We import the file ratings.csv which contains the variable “noncompliance” which
   corresponds to the measure NONCOMP defined in Appendix A. This dataset also
   contains a unique auditor identifier “personnelnumber” and year identifier
   “yearidentifier”. We merge these data onto panelY.csv where “staffcode” is equal to

evidence.description: The narrative names hours.csv, its person/year/category/hour fields and measure aggregation.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
5. We import the file hours.csv which contains a unique auditor identifier
   “personnelnumber” and year identifier “yearidentifier”. We generate the variables PD,
   L&E, QC, RECRUIT, and MENTOR by assigning the value of “hoursfy” to each
   respective variable conditional upon the label in variable “category”. We also retrieve
   hours spent by technical consultants on the auditor’s audit engagements, CONSULT, by
   assigning the value of “hoursfy” to each respective variable conditional upon the label in
   variable “category”. We then aggregate each measure by “personnelnumber” and
   “yearidentifier” and then merge with panelY.csv where “staffcode” is equal to
   “personnelnumber” and “fiscalyear” is equal to “yearidentifier”.

   “grandtotal” for each “staffcodeel” and “fiscalyear”. We merge these data with

evidence.description: The narrative names listed.csv and its public measure and auditor/year keys.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf

9. We import the file listed.csv which contains the variable “public” that we use as our
      measure PUBLIC. This file also contains unique auditor identifier “staffcode” and

evidence.description: The narrative names expenses.csv and its client-expense log construction.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
10. We import the file expenses.csv which contains the variable “expenses” which we use to
       compute our measure of client entertainment expenses incurred. This file also contains a
       unique auditor identifier “staffcode” and a unique year identifier “fiscalyear”. We
       aggregate expenses by “staffcode” and “fiscalyear”. We then merge the aggregated
       expenses with panelY.csv where “staffcode” is equal to “staffcode” and “fiscalyear” is
       equal to “fiscalyear”. We then take the log of this measure plus one to compute LNCE as
       defined in Appendix A.

evidence.description: The narrative names enghours.csv and industry-focus construction for the Firm Y panel.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
11. Lastly, we import the file enghours.csv which contains a unique auditor identifier
       “staffcodeel”, unique client industry identifier “clientindustrysector”, and a unique year
       “fiscalyear”. We aggregate the number of audit clients by “staffcodeel”
       “clientindustrysector” and “fiscalyear”. We code the client industry which represents the
       largest number of audit clients as the auditor’s client industry focus. We use this to
       generate AUTO, CONSUMER, TELECOM, FS, GOVERNMENT, SERVICES,
       CHEMICAL, ENERGY, CONSTRUCTION, HEALTHCARE, TRANSPORTATION,
       MANUFACTURING, and OTHER. We then merge these data onto panelY.csv to arrive at
       our final dataset for Firm Y firmYpanel.csv.

We merge the datasets firmXpanel.csv with firmYpanel.csv to arrive at the full sample file
fullsample.csv. After pooling the two samples we winsorize all continuous variables at the 1st and
99th percentile by “fiscalyear” to generate fullsample_win.csv.

TABLES

To conduct all statistical analyses we import the datasets into Stata.

evidence.description: The narrative reports sample exclusions but points to unprovided Section 3.3 for the audit-work threshold.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
•   In Panel A, we pool all potential observations. We remove 61 instances where there is a
       duplicate auditor-year observation, 55 without “audithours” data, 35 with negative
       “auditfees”, 17 with missing “comp”, two with “rank” below manager, one with no
       “clientrisk”, two with negative “tenure”, and 38 that do not engage in a sufficient level of
       audit work as discussed in Section 3.3.
   •   In Panel B, we only include observations from anonymous Firm X. We remove 25
       observations with missing “audithours” and 4 observations with negative “auditfees”. We
       remove 17 observations where “comp” is missing, two observations where “rank” is
       below manager, and two observations with negative “tenure”. Finally, we drop twelve
       auditor-years where the auditor does relatively no audit work as described in Section 3.3
       of the registered report.
   •   In Panel C, we only include observations from anonymous Firm Y. We drop 61 with
       duplicate auditor-years, 30 with missing “audithours”, 31 with missing “auditfees”, one
       with no “clientrisk”, and 26 that did an insufficient amount of audit work as described in
       Section 3.3.

evidence.description: The narrative identifies mixed-model analyses and the panel files used for Tables 4 and 5.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
TABLE 4: AUDITOR COMPENSATION AS A FUNCTION OF COMMERCIAL EFFORT
AND CONTROLS (H1)

Table 4 tabulates the results of our test of H1 where Columns (1) and (2) use the dataset
fullsample_win.csv, Column (3) uses firmXpanel.csv, and Column (4) uses firmYpanel.csv. We

then estimate our empirical model in Stata as an OLS regression with random auditor intercepts
and cluster standard errors by auditor using the mixed command.

TABLE 5: AUDIT TEAM EFFORT AS A FUNCTION OF AUDITOR COMMERCIAL
EFFORT AND CONTROLS (H2)

Table 5 presents the results of our test of H2 where Columns (1) and (2) use the dataset
fullsample_win.csv, Column (3) uses firmXpanel.csv, and Column (4) uses firmYpanel.csv. We
estimate an OLS regression with random auditor intercepts and cluster standard errors by auditor
using the mixed command.

evidence.description: The narrative identifies gsem analyses and panel use for the main and additional audit-quality analyses.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
TABLE 6: AUDIT QUALITY AS A FUNCTION OF AUDITOR COMMERCIAL EFFORT,
QUALITY CONTROL AND CONTROLS (H3a and H3b)

Table 6 presents the results from our tests of H3a and H3B. Panels A and D use
fullsample_win.csv, Panels B and E use firmXpanel.csv, and Panels C and F use firmYpanel.csv.
We estimate our structural equation model using gsem in Stata and include random auditor
intercepts as well as cluster standard errors by “staffcode”.

TABLE 7: ADDITIONAL ANALYSES OF AUDIT QUALITY AS A FUNCTION OF
AUDITOR COMMERICAL EFFORT, QUALITY CONTROL, AND CONTROLS

Table 7 presents the results from our tests of H3a and H3B. Panels A and B use
fullsample_win.csv. This table includes alternative measures of quality control, CONSULT_ACC
and CONSULT_AUD. We estimate our structural equation model using gsem in Stata and include
random auditor intercepts as well as cluster standard errors by “staffcode”.

evidence.description: The narrative describes the EVAL analysis in Table 8 using the fullsample_win.csv file and gsem.
evidence.file: CLW step by step data description.pdf
evidence.quote:
TABLE 8: ADDITIONAL ANALYSES OF AUDIT QUALITY AS A FUNCTION OF
AUDITOR COMMERCIAL EFFORT, QUALITY CONTROL, AND CONTROLS

Table 8 presents the results from our additional tests of H3a and H3B. Using fullsample_win.csv
and measuring audit quality with EVAL we estimate our structural equation model using gsem in
Stata and include random auditor intercepts as well as cluster standard errors by “staffcode”.

steps: Obtain author clarification or an authorized code/environment route; do not reconstruct the workflow independently.

Confirm every required file/field, auditor and year identifiers, sample-year coverage, and whether any full analysis panels are available. Proprietary history is not independently rebuilt.
steps: Use only an authorized FAR/author route; the current package itself contains no data tables.

review_notes: Provisional checkpoint after reading both supplied author documents and the complete registered inventory. The step-by-step narrative describes a SAS data-construction path and Stata analyses but supplies no executable code or dataset. Historical internal finance, HR and engagement systems are not being treated as independent reconstruction tasks.

No standalone program or formula-bearing workbook is included in the registered two-PDF inventory. The narrative describes preparation and analysis steps, but it does not supply an executable program, spreadsheet formulas, or a click-by-click GUI sequence.
Frozen title and document title differ only in wording/capitalization; no material attribution conflict or DOI conflict is established from the supplied documents.
The documents' titles match the frozen paper title in identity; capitalization and phrasing differ slightly, and neither supplied document states a conflicting DOI.

The static audit listed the same two PDFs by matching hashes and zero code edges, but its root field points to a different historical package location. It was used only as discovery context; assigned work-item paths and sources remain authoritative.

The registered environment artifact was viewed only through the checksum-verified typed viewer. It reports Stata 18 available and SAS unverified. The original environment JSON remains the cited probe; the viewer projection is not treated as a new probe. No SAS process was started.

The narrative names no mandatory standard commercial product or public data product; no catalog lookup or public-route check was applicable. No historical-source reconstruction or independent data hunt was performed.
No separate analysis_only scope is supported: the package supplies neither analysis-ready data nor an analysis program. The final target remains the full author-documented workflow.
